"I attended the match 20 years ago and the passing years do not diminish the importance and the poignancy of this occasion." Taylor was deeply critical of the police operation at Hillsborough, but his most significant recommendations were the removal of perimeter fencing and the creation of all-seater stadia. His report also cleared Liverpool fans of blame for the tragedy after lurid tabloid headlines provoked revulsion on Merseyside. Prime minister Gordon Brown paid reference to the controversy in an interview released on Liverpool's official television channel. "It was wrong for people to blame, as some did, Liverpool fans on that day," he said. "That's probably what matters most -- that people understood that the behavior of Liverpool fans in helping each other was magnificent. "Let's never forget the fans who cruelly lost their lives on a day when we know the people of Liverpool were trying to help each other," he added. However, the people of Liverpool are still angry and bitter at the lack of justice for those who died -- and that frustration surfaced when Andy Burnham, the   Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport took to the stand to address the crowd. As Burnham spoke, the crowd rose as one to sing "Justice for the 96". The Kop chant boomed around the stadium and Burnham, an Everton fan, was left in no doubt about the strength of feeling over the lack of accountability from officialdom over the tragedy. Fittingly, the ceremony was concluded with Gerry Marsden leading the fans in singing Liverpool anthem 'You'll Never Walk Alone'.

# Liverpool Falls Silent as City Marks Hillsborough Anniversary With Emotion, Resolve

**LIVERPOOL, England** — The city of Liverpool came to a standstill Thursday as thousands gathered to remember the 97 men, women and children who lost their lives in the Hillsborough disaster, in a memorial service that blended raw grief with renewed calls for justice.

Bells tolled across the city at the exact moment the fatal crush began during the 1989 FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield's Hillsborough Stadium. For a full minute, shops closed their doors, buses paused in the streets, and conversations stopped as the city observed a silence that has become a solemn annual ritual.

At Anfield, Liverpool FC's historic stadium, family members of the victims gathered alongside club officials, local dignitaries and supporters at the Hillsborough Memorial, where 97 names are etched in stone alongside the words "You'll Never Walk Alone."

"Every year it doesn't get easier — if anything, the weight of it grows heavier," said Margaret Aspinall, whose 18-year-old son James was among those who died and who has become one of the most prominent voices in the decades-long fight for accountability. "But we come back because we owe it to them. We owe it to the 97 to never let the world forget what happened, and why it happened."

The memorial service featured readings of each victim's name, a tradition maintained since the disaster, followed by hymns and reflections from faith leaders representing multiple denominations across the city.

## A City Transformed by Tragedy

Liverpool's Mayor addressed the gathered crowd, describing Hillsborough not just as a footballing tragedy but as a defining moment in the city's modern identity.

"Hillsborough changed us," the mayor said. "It changed how we see ourselves, how we fight for one another, and how we refuse to accept injustice when we see it. The families of the 97 taught this entire city — and frankly, this entire country — what dignity in the face of institutional failure looks like."

The disaster, which unfolded amid severe overcrowding in stadium pens, was for years wrongly attributed by some officials and portions of the press to the behavior of Liverpool fans themselves — a narrative that inflicted additional decades of pain on grieving families and survivors. Subsequent inquiries and inquests have since established that failures in policing and stadium safety were to blame, vindicating families who had campaigned for years against the initial findings.

## Fans Reflect on Legacy

Among the crowds at Anfield were supporters too young to have witnessed the disaster firsthand but who said they felt a responsibility to carry its memory forward.

"My dad used to tell me about that day, how it felt like the whole city stopped breathing," said one young supporter, wrapped in a red-and-white scarf despite the spring chill. "I never experienced it myself, but it's part of who we are as fans, as a city. You come here and you understand why it matters so much, still, all these years later."

Older supporters, some of whom had been at Hillsborough themselves, described the day with a heaviness that has never fully lifted.

"I lost friends that day," said one man in his sixties, declining to give his name. "You never really recover. You just learn to carry it. Coming here every year, standing with everyone else who understands — that's the only thing that helps."

## Calls for Continued Accountability

Officials and campaigners used the anniversary to renew calls for full accountability and systemic reform, noting that the long struggle for truth had reshaped public understanding of institutional transparency in Britain.

"The fight for justice took decades longer than it should have," said a representative of the Hillsborough Family Support Group. "We are here today to honor the 97, yes — but also to insist that no other families should ever have to fight so hard, for so long, simply to be told the truth."

As the service concluded, supporters linked arms and sang "You'll Never Walk Alone," the anthem long associated with Liverpool FC that has taken on deeper resonance in the context of the tragedy — a hymn not just to football, but to solidarity, memory and endurance.

The disaster remains one of the deadliest incidents in the history of European sport and a pivotal moment that led to sweeping changes in stadium safety standards across the United Kingdom, including the elimination of standing terraces at top-flight venues.

For Liverpool, though, Thursday's service was a reminder that beyond the policy changes and legal reckonings, the anniversary remains, first and foremost, a day of mourning — one the city continues to hold with both sorrow and unwavering solidarity.
